A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching tasks, architectures and symbolic programs. Their text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural-network training experiments, causal intervention accuracies, activation analyses and learning trajectories in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original training and intervention results, including orthogonal versus linear DAS comparisons, subspace-size experiments and transformer analyses.

M1.justification: V2 Section 3.4 extends orthogonal DAS with a learned invertible alignment X(h+b), including a bias and inverse transformation for interventions. This changes the alignment procedure substantially. The three symbolic programs remain; Last Value becoming Input Value is principally a rename.

E1.justification: The represented tasks remain Multi-Object, Single-Object, Same-Object, their void-token Variable-Length variants, and the simplified task without BOS and trigger tokens. These already appear in v1. Expanded architecture and alignment comparisons change configurations and analyses rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: V1 Figure 4 compares Up-Down, Up-Up and Ctx-Distr across all three architectures. V2's recurrent comparisons omit Ctx-Distr, while its transformer Count/Input Value comparisons omit Up-Up. The GRU reference in v1 Figure 9 is also absent from the corresponding transformer comparison in v2 Figure 6.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 changes default state size from 20 to 128 and maximum model learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001. DAS learning rate changes from 0.003 to 0.001; Section 3.4 replaces fixed half-width interventions with selection between 16 dimensions and half-width. The stated accuracy cutoff and continuation-sampling rules also change. These establish reported protocol revisions, not independently verified reruns.

E4.justification: V2 adds alignment-function comparisons, small-subspace sensitivity tests and causal decompositions of neural activity. It removes v1's PCA case studies and attention-output substitution tests for localizing the EOS decision. The existing strength-value interventions are extended across transformer configurations, and gradience analyses now emphasize 128-dimensional GRUs and phase-specific comparisons.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 changes the reported number of training seeds per condition from six to five, with revised exclusion counts. Both versions already display error bars and shaded bands; no new confidence-interval construction or significance-testing procedure is specified.

E6.justification: V2 adds linear and one-dimensional DAS results, including Same-Object GRU Count IIA of 0.991 with linear alignment. RoPE token-value IIAs change from 0.827/0.960 to 0.800/0.935 for Multi-Object/Variable-Length Multi-Object under revised settings, rather than demonstrating comparable-setting declines. V2 Section 4.2.3 and Figure 6 identify these conditions despite Table 3's inconsistent Same-Object column heading.

T1.justification: V2 adds alignment-function mathematics and an activity-component derivation in Equations 6–9, plus a transformer state-propagation argument and formal theorem/proof in Appendix A.6. The single-layer NoPE strength-value derivation already existed in v1 Appendix A.4 and is largely relocated to the main text.

C1.justification: V2 makes generalizing DAS a principal contribution and claims that transformers must use anti-Markovian solutions across tasks without sufficient attention layers. V1 explicitly expressed uncertainty about generalizing its transformer finding beyond counting. The abstract and contribution list consequently shift toward alignment functions and a general architectural claim.

C2.justification: V2 introduces nonorthogonal subspaces and linear combinations of count variables as explanations for improved alignment. It adds a scratchpad/chain-of-thought qualification and acknowledges that sampled continuations are not strictly counterfactual. Earlier overlap/PCA explanations, lottery-ticket/lazy-learning speculation and the children's number-cognition analogy are removed.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new alignment parameterization and initialization, and substantially expands intervention construction in Appendix A.3.3–A.3.7. Worked source/target/counterfactual examples, invalid-sample restrictions and gradience-evaluation sampling make the procedures more reproducible. Newly disclosed restrictions do not by themselves establish changes to previously undocumented implementation.

R1.justification: The central related-work survey remains. V2 adds Haviv et al. on positional information, Nye et al. on scratchpads and Wei et al. on chain-of-thought, while removing citations supporting the lottery-ticket/NTK, RASP-L and child-number discussions. It also positions the work as extending DAS rather than only applying it.

P1.justification: The abstract and contributions are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized into recurrent-network and transformer sections, much of the former discussion is integrated into those sections, and the conclusion is shortened. The appendices are restructured around intervention examples and the new proof.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the main comparisons around orthogonal/linear alignment and replaces PCA/conceptual panels with aligned activity visualizations. It adds three numbered result tables, intervention-example tables and sensitivity plots, while regrouping performance and attention figures. Typography, author presentation and text-block layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: Linear DAS, its ablations and the worked intervention examples improve the investigation of v1's unresolved Same-Object failures. However, the new general transformer claim relies on a theorem that assumes its key depth/state condition in Appendix A.6. Section 4.1.4 also retains a poor-Same-Object-alignment interpretation despite Table 1's LSTM orthogonal Count IIA of 0.958. These methodological gains and central support/consistency problems leave the overall quality direction uncertain.
